title: Clothing Swap & Thrift Math
tagline: Sort · Price · Find the real value
goal: Your kid goes through their closet, works out what their clothes are really worth, and then runs a clothing swap with friends or shops a thrift store on a small budget. Along the way they calculate cost per wear, price their own items, and find out exactly how much secondhand saves.
need: Your kid's closet, or one drawer of it
Paper, a pencil and a calculator
A thrift store, a friends-and-family swap, or both
Optional: a small thrift budget, $5 to $15

lesson.text: "Cheap" isn't a number. A percentage tells you how good a deal really is, and cost per wear tells you if it was worth it.
lesson.before: It was cheap, like half off.

model.line: $34 ÷ $40 = 0.85, so 85% off. Way better than half.
An 85% saving on something you'll actually wear. That's a real deal.

lesson.modelNote: 'Half off' was a guess. Dividing the saving by the new price gives 85%, and asking 'will I wear it?' decides if it's a deal at all.

academics.subject: Math
academics.text: division, percentages, adding and subtracting money

academics.subject: Money
academics.text: budgets, fair prices, new versus secondhand

howTo.intro: Keep your opinions about their clothes to yourself, even about the hoodie you've wanted gone for a year. What stays and what goes is their call. Keep it cheap too: a swap is free, and a thrift trip needs only a few dollars.

plan.what: Audit the closet and work out cost per wear (Steps 1 and 2).
Price the swap pile and plan the swap or the thrift trip (Steps 3 and 4).
Do it, then compare new and secondhand and add up the savings (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.q: They won't let go of anything
troubleshoot.a: That's fine. Don't push. The cost-per-wear maths often changes their mind on its own, and keeping things is a decision too.
Swap within the family, or skip the swap and do the thrift trip. Pricing the pile still works for a donation or a garage sale.

steps.title: Audit the closet
steps.why: Knowing what you own before deciding what's worth anything.
steps.kid: Your kid goes through their clothes, all of them or one section at a time, and sorts every item into four piles: keep, swap, donate, sell. They count each pile and rate the condition of everything leaving: excellent, good or fair.
steps.you: Let them make every call. Ask 'when did you last wear this?' and 'does it still fit?', but don't push them to give away things they love.
ask: How many things haven't you worn in 3 months?
What makes something worth swapping instead of donating?
steps.tip: Lay the piles out on the bed or the floor. Seeing the size of each one is half the lesson.

levels.explore: Sort at least 15 items into the 4 piles and count each pile.
levels.develop: Sort everything, count it and rate the condition of everything leaving.
levels.extend: How many t-shirts get you to laundry day? Compare that with how many you own.

steps.title: Work out cost per wear
steps.why: The real price of a piece of clothing is what it costs each time you wear it.
steps.kid: Your kid picks 5 to 10 items, a mix of favourites and things they hardly wear. For each one they write the price (or an estimate) and how many times they've worn it, then divide: price ÷ wears = cost per wear. Which item was the best value, and which was the worst?
steps.you: Help them estimate prices and wears if they don't remember: once a week, once a month, just once? The guess only needs to be reasonable.
ask: A $25 jacket worn 50 times: what does each wear cost?
Is your best-value item the one you expected?
steps.tip: The surprise is usually the favourite hoodie that cost the most and turns out to be the cheapest per wear.

levels.explore: Tally wears for 5 items. Of two that cost the same, which was the better buy?
levels.develop: Do 10 items, rank them best to worst, and explain what makes good value.
levels.extend: How many wears would something you want new need to match your best-value item's cost per wear?

steps.title: Price the swap pile
steps.why: Pricing is part maths, part judgement.
steps.kid: Your kid sets a fair price on every item they're swapping or selling. They use the condition rating and look up what similar things sell for at a thrift store or a secondhand site. Then they write one line explaining each price.
steps.you: Ask 'would you pay that for it?' and 'why is this one worth more than that one?' Help them check real secondhand prices, in a store or online.
ask: Would a small stain or a missing button change the price?
If the same brand sells for $8 at the thrift store, is $10 fair?
steps.tip: Most kids price their own things too high at first. Real reference prices bring the numbers down fast.

levels.explore: Sort 5 to 10 items into $1, $3 and $5 piles by condition.
levels.develop: Price everything, check 3 to 5 real reference prices, and explain each price.
levels.extend: Should 'fair' mean $2 off or a third off? Test both on a $3 tee and a $15 jacket.

steps.title: Swap or shop
steps.why: Real decisions about value, with real people and real money.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a clothing swap, a thrift trip, or both. For a swap, they set the rules for fair trades (the point system in the Value Guide at the end of the guide helps) and invite people. For a thrift trip, they set a budget and a needs list. Then they do it and record every trade or purchase.
steps.you: Help with the logistics, then let them run it. At the store, ask 'need or want?' and 'did you check it for stains and holes?' At a swap, ask 'was that trade fair for both sides?'
ask: Your item is worth 3 points and theirs is worth 1. How do you make it fair?
How much of your budget is left?
steps.tip: Have them check every thrift find against the Quality Check before it goes in the basket.

levels.explore: Plan and do a simple family swap or a short thrift trip, and draw or write what you got.
levels.develop: Set swap rules or a budget and needs list, and keep a running total.
levels.extend: With 3 or more swappers, set 1 point per $3 of thrift price and keep a ledger. Do the points balance?

steps.title: Compare new and secondhand
steps.why: Where percentages prove whether secondhand was worth it.
steps.kid: For 3 to 5 things they got, your kid looks up the price new and works out the saving and the percentage off. Then they predict how many times they'll wear each one, find the predicted cost per wear, and add up the totals: spent, saved, and items given a second life.
steps.you: Help them look up new prices. Ask 'is the secondhand one just as good?' and 'if you did this every season, how much would you save in a year?'
ask: A $40 jacket for $10: how much did you save, and what percentage off is that?
Which find will be the best value a few months from now?
steps.tip: Have them write the yearly total big at the bottom of the page. It's usually a number that surprises the whole family.

levels.explore: For 3 items, count up from the thrift price to the new price to find what you saved.
levels.develop: Compare 5 items with savings and percentages, and rank them by biggest saving.
levels.extend: By cost per wear, when does a bargain you'll rarely wear lose to a full-price item you wear all the time?

reference.title: Value Guide
reference.intro: Ballpark numbers for pricing and swapping. Prices vary a lot by store, so real local prices always win.

items.name: Condition

lines.v: looks new, no marks, no fading
worn but clean, no holes or stains
small marks, some fading, still wearable

items.ask: Would you be happy to get this in a swap?

items.name: Thrift ballpark prices
items.ask: Do 3 prices from a store near you match these?

items.name: Swap points

lines.v: trade equal points, or add a small item to even it out

items.ask: Would both people call the trade fair?

items.name: Quality check

lines.v: check the cuffs, the collar and the front
hold it up to the light
try it on, or measure against something that fits

items.ask: Does it pass all five before you pay?

after.label: The thrift maths
lines: Cost per wear = price ÷ number of wears

conclusion.headline: Half off turned out to be 85% off.
conclusion.text: Hold up two shirts from the keep pile and ask which one was the better buy. Expect an answer about how often each one got worn, not which one was cheaper.
conclusion.celebrate: As they show you their best find, say it back: 'Six dollars, and you'll wear it all winter. Better than most of my closet.'
extensions: Do a closet audit every season and watch how cost per wear changes
Run a bigger swap with a few families and a shared point system
Compare three ways to buy: new, thrift store and a secondhand app
Count how many items the swap kept out of the garbage this year

signs: They check the tag before they check the price
They work out cost per wear in their head
They suggest a swap before asking for something new
makeItReal: When your kid needs something, like a jacket for the season, hand them the thrift budget and let them find it. Afterward, look up the new price together and work out the percentage they saved.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.
